title: Getting Started with the OpenAI API: A Developer's Guide
description: From API key to first streaming chatbot: authentication, chat completions, structured output, function calling, error handling, and keeping costs under control.

author: MyAppAI Team

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: The OpenAI API is the fastest way to add language-model capabilities to an application: no model hosting, no GPU management, just HTTPS calls. This guide takes you from a fresh API key to a working integration with streaming, structured output, and sane cost controls — plus the error handling that separates a demo from production code.

sections.heading: Setup and Authentication
sections.body:
Create an account at platform.openai.com, add a payment method (the API is usage-based; there's no free tier for API calls beyond initial trial credits), and generate an API key from the API keys page. Set a spending limit immediately — in the dashboard under Billing → Limits. This is the single most important setup step; an accidental infinite loop calling the API is an expensive lesson.

Store the key in an environment variable, never in source code:

```bash export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..." ```

Install the official SDK:

```bash npm install openai ```

```js import OpenAI from 'openai'; const client = new OpenAI(); // reads OPENAI_API_KEY automatically ```

Security note: the API key must only live on your server. Any key shipped in client-side JavaScript can be extracted in seconds. If you need model access from a browser or mobile app, route it through your own backend endpoint.

sections.heading: Your First Completion
sections.body:
```js const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o', messages: [ { role: 'system', content: 'You are a concise, helpful assistant.' }, { role: 'user', content: 'Explain REST APIs in two sentences.' }, ], });

console.log(response.choices[0].message.content); ```

Three concepts here that matter for everything after:

Messages form a conversation: `system` sets behavior, `user` provides input, `assistant` holds prior replies. To maintain context across turns, send the full message history each call — the API is stateless. The system prompt is where you define the assistant's role, tone, and constraints. Time spent writing a good one pays off more than model upgrades. Model selection is a cost/quality tradeoff. Flagship models handle nuance and complex reasoning; smaller models (like the mini variants) are dramatically cheaper and fine for classification, extraction, and simple generation. Default to the smaller model and upgrade only where quality demands it.

sections.heading: Streaming Responses
sections.body:
Waiting for a full response before showing anything feels broken in a chat UI. Stream tokens as they generate:

```js const stream = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Write a haiku about APIs.' }], stream: true, });

for await (const chunk of stream) { process.stdout.write(chunk.choices[0]?.delta?.content || ''); } ```

On the frontend, append each chunk to the displayed text. Handle the stream ending cleanly — network interruptions mid-stream are normal, so your UI should distinguish "still generating" from "failed" and offer a retry.

sections.heading: Structured Output
sections.body:
When you need the model to return data your code can parse — not prose — ask for JSON explicitly. Modern models support constrained output:

```js const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o', messages: [ { role: 'system', content: 'Extract the meeting details as JSON.' }, { role: 'user', content: 'Lunch with Priya tomorrow at noon at Cafe Luna' }, ], response_format: { type: 'json_schema', json_schema: { name: 'meeting', schema: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' }, attendee: { type: 'string' }, time: { type: 'string' }, location: { type: 'string' }, }, required: ['title', 'time'], }, }, }, });

const meeting = JSON.parse(response.choices[0].message.content); ```

Validate the parsed result against your schema anyway. Constrained output is highly reliable but not a substitute for validation at the boundary.

sections.heading: Function Calling: Letting the Model Use Your Tools
Error Handling for Production
sections.body:
The API fails in predictable ways; handle each:

429 rate limits — back off exponentially and retry. Set `max_retries` on the client (it defaults to 2) and add jitter. 401 authentication — your key is wrong or revoked. Fail loudly; retrying won't help. Context length exceeded — your prompt plus history exceeds the model's window. Trim old messages (keep the system prompt and recent turns) or summarize history. Timeouts — set explicit timeouts on requests and treat a timeout as retryable.

Log the request ID from error responses — support can't help you without it.

sections.heading: Controlling Costs
sections.body:
API spend scales with tokens, and tokens scale with sloppy prompts. Practical controls:

Spending limits in the dashboard — set monthly caps per project. Right-size the model per task; classification rarely needs the flagship. Cache aggressively — identical prompts (system prompts, few-shot examples) shouldn't be re-sent when avoidable. Limit max_tokens on every call; unbounded completions are how bills surprise you. Monitor per-feature usage with separate API keys per environment or feature, so one runaway feature is visible immediately.

A common pattern: prototype with the best model, then measure whether the cheaper model is good enough for each specific call site. Most production systems end up with a mix.

sections.heading: What to Build First
sections.body: Good first projects: a support-draft assistant (drafts replies for human approval), a document summarizer over your own content, or a classification pipeline (route tickets, tag content). All three have clear success criteria and a human in the loop — the two properties that make early AI integrations safe to learn on.
